title: Cold-path token siphon — field notes
content:
Context:
This is a personal scratchpad capturing experiments around an unusual tail-latency pattern we saw in the field: occasional long tails when a small fraction of requests traverse the "cold path" (cold KV cache / cold attention cache population) and appear to "siphon" tokens into long-lived operations. Aim is to get reproducible bench runs, quick numbers, and proposed mitigations.

Why I care:
- Customers report intermittent p99 spikes that don't correlate with aggregate QPS or GPU saturation.
- Hypothesis: small percentage of requests hit an execution path that triggers expensive synchronous KV cache writes / large prefill and blocks batching windows.

Environment (testbed):
- Model: small-llama-ish-7B-qat (cpu/gpu fused kernel profile)
- Fleet: 4x A100-40GB (dev pool), cuda 12.2, serving-runtime branch: token-siphon-expts-2024
- Config: dynamic batching on, max_batch_size=32, batch_timeout_ms=12, kv_cache_enabled=true, kv_cache_mode=local-memory
- Workload generator: custom harness (python) that replays real-arrival traces; also wrk/latency for microbench.
- Seed corpus: 80/20 short/long prompts, long prompts mean 512 tokens predicted.

Test plan (short):
1) Baseline: warm-run (run for 10m to populate caches) at steady 120 qps, measure p50/p95/p99, kv_hit_rate, batch sizes.
2) Cold path injection: randomly mark 2% of requests as "cold" by clearing their context id before send (simulate miss on prefix/KV). Measure spike behaviour.
3) Isolated cold spike: issue 1 cold request every 10s and watch tail correlation.
4) Mitigation probes: increase batch_timeout to 18ms, prefill async, and a version with kv_cache_mode=shared.

Commands (quick):
- Start harness: python bench/harness_replay.py --model small-llama-7b --qps 120 --seed-trace traces/oct09 --clients 32
- Cold injection: bench/harness_replay.py --cold-pct 2 --evict-on-send
- Collect metrics: curl http://obs-agent/metrics | grep kv_cache

Results (annotated):
Run A — baseline warm (10m steady)
- QPS: 120
- p50: 38ms, p95: 62ms, p99: 112ms
- avg batch size: 12.4
- kv_cache_hit_rate: 97.6%
- notes: stable, rare outliers ~1/min (GC pause correlates with host CPU nice value)

Run B — cold-pct=2% (burst over 10m)
- QPS: 120 overall
- p50: 40ms, p95: 75ms, p99: 420ms (heavy tail)
- avg batch size: 10.9 (drop)
- kv_cache_hit_rate: 94.8% (temporary dips to 70% right after cold events)
- observation: p99 spikes align within 10–15ms after cold injection. Allocation profile shows large synchronous slab allocations inside kv cache write path.

Micro-run C — single cold every 10s
- p99 baseline (no cold): 115ms
- when cold request occurs: we see a secondary p99 at ~380–520ms that persists for ~1s after the cold request (affects subsequent warm requests)
- trace snippet (timing for 3 requests):
  T0: warm request A processed, batch formed (size 12) -> 45ms
  T0+10ms: cold request B arrives, backend performs full prefill -> 410ms
  T0+20ms: warm request C arrives and joins same scheduling window -> blocked behind B, completes at ~420ms

Quick flame/prof notes:
- Hot path: attention kernel ~40% of time on long sequences; unchanged between runs.
- Cold path: kv_cache write + prefill + metadata lock account for ~280ms in cold request.
- Allocation: single large contiguous buffer allocate (1–2MB) each cold event, using host memory; free happens synchronously.

Hypotheses:
1) Blocking prefill + synchronous KV write holds scheduling mutex and prevents fast batching windows from servicing other requests, causing token siphon effect.
2) Large synchronous allocations cause page faults/compaction on host, adding 200–400ms.
3) Cold path requests are not prioritized and thus get mixed into shared batch windows; once in, they degrade other requests.

Mitigation experiments tried:
M1: batch_timeout_ms increased to 18ms
- Result: average batch size +1.6, p99 reduced from 420ms -> 220ms for cold-injection run. Good but increases p50 by ~5ms.
M2: kv_cache write made async (fire-and-forget) with best-effort retry
- Result: cold request p99 dropped to ~180–200ms; subsequent warm requests not blocked. Slight increase in background CPU usage.
M3: pre-allocate per-thread slab for prefill (avoid sync malloc)
- Result: removed 200–300ms allocation tail; p99 overall ~150ms. Stable in stress runs (30m).
M4: tag cold requests with high-priority so they are dispatched to a dedicated fast-path lane (no mixing)
- Result: warm requests unaffected but cold requests still heavy; overall customer-visible p99 improves. Needs scheduling infra changes.

Tradeoffs / concerns:
- Async KV writes risk temporary inconsistency if a node crashes before write completes; need idempotency guarantees.
- Increasing batch_timeout affects latency for all requests; acceptable for some customers, not for strict p50 SLAs.
- Dedicated cold lane increases resource footprint and may lower throughput efficiency.

Immediate next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Push a small pre-alloc slab prototype (M3) to internal branch and run 24h stress
- [ ] Add instrumentation: track "requests that triggered prefill" and correlate to host malloc stats (jemalloc samples)
- [ ] Small experiment to mark cold requests as separate QoS class in dev cluster (M4) — Spike PR: gh/427 linked above
- [ ] Write a short runbook for SRE on how to detect token-siphon events from metrics (kv_cache_write_latency, batch_size_drop, p99 spikes after evict events)

Notes for oncall / SRE detection heuristics:
- Alert if kv_cache_hit_rate drops >10% for >30s and p99 > 3x baseline
- Quick check: run sample trace: run 10 cold requests and monitor downstream host malloc rate.

Ideas for longer-term:
- Move kv cache writes to a background append-only log on NVMe, with async flush; that should avoid blocking and large host allocs.
- Consider per-tenant cold-lane scheduling for cold-starts with prefetch (if tenant-specific models are common)
- Metric: introduce "siphon-index" = fraction of requests that cause >200ms add-on latency within next 1s window; track over time.

Raw numbers appendix (aggregated):
- Baseline warm: p50 38ms, p95 62ms, p99 112ms
- Cold 2%: p50 40ms, p95 75ms, p99 420ms
- M1 (batch_timeout 18): p99 220ms
- M2 (async kv write): p99 ~190ms
- M3 (prealloc slab): p99 ~150ms

Personal take: the token "siphon" effect is a scheduling/alloc problem, not a model compute one. Fast fixes (prealloc, async KV writes) give large wins and are low-risk to try in dev. QoS/dedicated lane is the cleanest but costlier.

Log of quick runs (timestamps):
- 2024-11-07 10:12 start baseline-run-A
- 2024-11-07 10:25 baseline-run-A metrics dump attached
- 2024-11-09 14:04 cold-2pct run-B started (eviction script v0.3)
- 2024-11-10 09:22 micro-run-C single-cold-every-10s
- 2024-12-01 16:10 M3 prototype prealloc run

Attach: I'll paste minimal flame snippets & jemalloc stats into Confluence INF-3421 and link — see linked_artifacts.

Questions to answer in follow-ups:
- If we adopt async kv writes, what is the failure window for durability? (ask storage/infra)
- Could we detect "coldness" earlier (client side) and pre-warm automatically? (solutions-eng)
- Cost model for dedicated cold lane vs p99 reduction: run a capacity simulation.

End of notes.
(Feel free to copy into an internal writeup if we want to escalate to product.)
